extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners interested in philosophy of science and methods of induction; scientists reflecting on justification of generalizations
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for forming, testing, and accepting inductive generalizations in science, including the role and justification of the law of causation and limits of methods for co-existence claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer universal causation from single-instance proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A demonstration that in a particular instance B could have had no other cause than A proves only that in that instance B had no other cause; to conclude that A is the cause in general, or will be followed by B on other occasions, assumes the universality of the law of causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware petitio principii: establishing that A was the only antecedent in one case does not by itself justify asserting A as the general cause unless one already assumes that every event must have a cause that recurs. Explicitly recognize and justify any move from a singular causal instance to a universal causal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief/instinct is not evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The disposition of the human mind to believe in the universality of causation (or any proposition) is not proof of its truth; belief is not proof and does not dispense with the necessity of external evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not appeal to the ubiquity of a belief as justification for a factual claim; instead appeal from the judging faculty to faculties that take cognizance of fact (sense and consciousness). Treat instinctive conviction as a psychological fact, not as epistemic warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper meaning of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence is not everything that produces belief, but that which it ought to yield to—i.e., that which, by yielding to it, keeps belief conformable to fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims, distinguish causes of belief (association, instinct) from genuine evidence; require that evidence be such that reasonable judgment tends to make belief track reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple enumeration is fallible but sometimes useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction 'per enumerationem simplicem' (simple enumeration) is a valid but fallible form of induction; it provides varying degrees of assurance depending on the breadth of the generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize a scale of trustworthiness in results from simple enumeration: extremely general claims are more precarious when derived from few instances, while very broad and repeatedly confirmed regularities can be provisionally accepted within limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific induction improves by deriving or testing generalizations against stronger inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: The improvement of induction consists in correcting inartificial generalizations by means of other generalizations; to test a generalization is to show that it either follows from, or conflicts with, some stronger induction resting on a broader foundation of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer to accept generalizations that are supported by broader, stronger inductions (or shown inconsistent with them). Use higher-order generalizations and the Four Methods of Induction to strengthen or refute narrower claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of sufficient coincidences versus chance
rubrics_metrics.description: A fact observed a certain number of times and never known to be false may be affirmed as an empirical law true within certain limits, provided the number of coincidences is greater than can with any probability be ascribed to chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding to accept an empirical law from repeated observation, weigh whether the observed coincidences exceed what chance would plausibly produce; limit the law's scope to the time, place, and circumstances warranted by the observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit empirical generalizations to observed ranges (time/place/circumstance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations inferred from observation should be regarded as empirical laws true within certain limits of time, place, and circumstance; do not extend them beyond those limits without further evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the contextual bounds of a generalization. Avoid unwarranted extrapolation to distant or qualitatively different domains (e.g., distant stellar regions) where experience provides no ground for estimating probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of causation as a higher-order sanction for narrower inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of causation, being the most extensive generalization about sequences of phenomena, can impart its certainty to other inductive propositions: narrower inductions gain ultimate sanction when connected to the universal law that every event has a cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, relate special laws to the broader law of causation; treat subordinate generalizations as proved only to the extent that the law of causation confirms them. Use the universal law to explain apparent exceptions (via counteracting causes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile apparent exceptions via counteracting causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent exceptions to special causal laws often serve to confirm the universal law when they can be traced to absence of a usual cause or presence of a counteracting cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate exceptions for hidden or counteracting causes before rejecting a general causal law. Use this reconciliation as evidence strengthening the universal causal principle when exceptions are thus accounted for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain provisional certainty and openness to refutation
rubrics_metrics.description: Even our strongest inductive convictions must leave an opening in the mind for facts which contradict them; hold convictions provisionally and act confidently only until an undoubted exception appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a fallibilist stance: act on well-established generalizations but be prepared to revise them if incontrovertible contrary evidence arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish uniformities of succession (causation) from uniformities of co-existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities of occurrence are either successive (governed by causation) or simultaneous (co-existence). Uniformities of succession fall under the law of causation; co-existence uniformities may or may not depend on causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating co-existence claims, determine whether the co-existence is a derivative law (effects of causes that co-exist) or concerns ultimate properties of kinds; apply methods appropriate to each case rather than conflating them with causal inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: When co-existence depends on causation treat it as an empirical law
rubrics_metrics.description: If co-existent properties are effects dependent on causes, the proposition asserting their co-existence is a derivative empirical law and should be tried by principles of induction applicable to empirical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject co-existence claims grounded in causal dependence to the same inductive scrutiny as other empirical laws (tests by methods of causation, search for counteracting factors, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-existences among ultimate properties define kinds and are not amenable to causal elimination
rubrics_metrics.description: If co-existing properties are ultimate (not results of causation), they are ultimate properties of the same Kind; asserting something of a Kind is asserting uniform co-existence of its identifying properties. There is no general axiom analogous to causation that allows elimination methods here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that for properties of Kinds there is no equivalent of the principle 'everything which has a beginning must have a cause'. Therefore do not expect methods like Agreement, Difference, or Concomitant Variations to be generally applicable to establish co-existence of ultimate properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat generalizations about kinds as potentially empirical unless shown ultimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Most properties of compounds and organized beings are presumptively dependent on causes; hence generalizations about kinds may be derivative and cannot be assumed ultimate without proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid granting ultimate status to co-existence generalizations by default. Investigate whether properties can be resolved into causal dependencies; if they are, treat the generalization as empirical and subject to inductive testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not apply Baconian elimination uncritically to co-existences
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon's application of the elimination principle to investigations of co-existence (forms) was mistaken: objects that agree in some general property seldom agree in other circumstances, so elimination often yields no result for co-existences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming that shared properties imply further common properties via elimination. Use methods suitable to the nature of the property (causal investigation vs. classificatory analysis) and be cautious about expecting invariable co-occurrences.
